title: Nominal relative clauses: what, whatever, whoever
summary: A nominal relative clause works like a whole noun phrase. It lets you make a clause the subject or object of a sentence, and is a key tool for emphasis and precise argument.
author: QEVRANT editorial (AI-assisted draft)

sections.title: From relative clause to noun phrase

blocks.text: In an ordinary relative clause, the clause describes a noun: *the thing that surprised me*. In a **nominal relative clause**, the noun and the relative word merge into one word, and the whole clause becomes a noun phrase: **what surprised me**.

items.en: The thing that surprised me was the cost. → **What surprised me** was the cost.
Anyone who finishes early can leave. → **Whoever finishes early** can leave.
You can choose any topic that interests you. → You can choose **whichever topic interests you**.

blocks.text: Because the clause is now a noun phrase, it can go anywhere a noun phrase goes: subject, object, complement, or after a preposition.

Meaning
Example
rows: anything that / it doesn't matter what
any one (from a known set) that
any place where / the place where
She studies **wherever she can find a quiet desk**.
any time that / every time that
in any way that / the way that
Organise your notes **however works for you**.

items.en: **What the data shows** is a steady decline.
I didn't understand **what the lecturer meant**.
That is exactly **what worries me**.
It depends on **what you mean by success**.

blocks.text: **What** already contains its noun. **That** and **which** need a noun before them. If there is a noun, you cannot use *what*; if there is no noun, you cannot use *that* or *which* as a relative.

items.en: ~~Everything what he said was true.~~
items.note: There is a noun (*everything*), so use *that*.

items.en: Everything **that** he said was true.
~~That he said was true.~~
items.note: No noun, so the clause needs *what*.

items.en: **What** he said was true.

blocks.text: *All what* is always wrong. Use **all (that)**: *All (that) you need is a library card.*

A *what*-clause followed by *be* lets you delay the key information until the end of the sentence, where English puts its focus. This structure is called a pseudo-cleft, and it is one of the most useful emphasis tools in academic writing and speaking.

items.en: The curriculum needs more flexibility. → **What the curriculum needs is** more flexibility.
**What I'm suggesting is that** we assess skills, not memory.
**What happened was that** the funding was cut in the middle of the project.
**What they did was (to) redesign** the whole first year.
items.note: *What + subject + did + was + (to) infinitive* focuses on an action.

blocks.text: In IELTS-style Speaking Part 3 and in essay conclusions, a pseudo-cleft is a natural way to signal your main point: *What really matters, in my view, is…*
The *-ever* words have two related uses. Keep them apart.

items: **As a noun phrase** (nominal relative): *Whoever designed this timetable* had never taught. = the person who …
**As a concession** (it doesn't matter …): *Whatever you decide, tell your supervisor early.* = No matter what you decide …

items.en: **Whichever university you choose**, the first year will be demanding.
**However hard the course is**, don't give up in the first month.
She'll succeed **wherever she goes**.
items.note: Concession at the end; no comma needed.

items.en: ~~What I need it is more time.~~
items.note: The *what*-clause is already the subject. → *What I need **is** more time.*

items.en: ~~What made me choose this course was because it was practical.~~
items.note: After *What … was*, use a noun phrase or a *that*-clause, not *because*. → *What made me choose this course **was that** it was practical.*

items.en: ~~I don't know what does she want.~~
items.note: No question word order inside the clause. → *I don't know what **she wants**.*

items.en: ~~Who arrives first should open the room.~~
items.note: Plain *who* cannot be a nominal relative in modern English. → ***Whoever** arrives first …*

blocks.text: Nominal relatives are neutral and appear in every register. Pseudo-clefts with *what* are especially common in speech and in argument writing. Very formal academic writing sometimes prefers a noun: *the extent to which*, *the way in which*, *the factors that*.

items.en: Neutral: Researchers disagree about **what causes** the gap.
More formal: Researchers disagree about **the factors that cause** the gap.

items: *what* = *the thing(s) that*; never after a noun or *all*.
A nominal relative clause is a noun phrase: subject, object, complement or after a preposition.
Use *What … is …* to move new information to the end for emphasis.
*whoever, whatever, whichever* can mean *anyone/anything that* or *no matter who/what/which*.
Use statement word order inside the clause.
